description: Vamos por field shift,  una herramienta que ayude a agricultores a elegir qué sembrar y en qué orden.
summary:
SafeSow is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web app that helps smallholder rice farmers in Ecuador's lower Guayas basin (Daule, Salitre, Samborondón and Babahoyo) decide what to sow before and after a flood. Ecuador's El Niño committee (CN-ERFEN) expects the strongest impact of El Niño between November 2026 and March 2027, exactly the rice-sowing season.

SafeSow combines 25 years of NASA POWER climate data, NASA MODIS NDVI satellite greenness and live NASA GIBS flood maps with FAO-56 crop water coefficients. It compares three rotation strategies month by month: the current rice–rice pattern, wet-season rice followed by dry-season soybean, and skipping wet-season rice on flood-prone plots. For each one it shows dry-season irrigation need, months a cash crop is exposed to flooding, bare-soil months, evidence, information gaps and risks to review with a local technician.

An "After the flood" planner shows what can still be sown and when, a "Learn" section with read-aloud cards supports farmers with low literacy, and a WhatsApp button shares the plan with their technician. The tool supports, and does not replace, the farmer's judgement.
details:
The problem

Around Daule, Salitre, Samborondón (Guayas) and Babahoyo (Los Ríos), most smallholder rice farmers repeat rice after rice and sow at the start of the rainy season (January–April). When El Niño brings extreme rain, young rice that stays under water for about a week can die and the whole investment is lost. Ecuador's CN-ERFEN committee expects the main impact of the 2026–27 El Niño between November 2026 and March 2027. Farmers need simple, local answers to two questions: which rotation lowers my risk this year? and after the flood, what can I still sow?

What SafeSow does

  • Your farm: choose one of four rice zones and a wet-season scenario (normal, or a "wetter than normal" what-if that multiplies January–April rain ×1.1–2.0; labelled as a scenario, not a forecast).
  • Live view from space: a map with NASA GIBS layers: MODIS 3-day near-real-time flood map, MODIS 16-day NDVI, IMERG rain rate, MODIS true colour, and the 1985–2003 flood hazard frequency grid.
  • Rain vs. crop water demand: monthly NASA POWER rain against reference evapotranspiration (ET0), showing when water is in excess and when irrigation is needed.
  • Compare 3 rotation strategies (S0 current rice + rice/ratoon; S1 rice → soybean; S2 water-tolerant cover → irrigated dry-season rice) with a 12-month calendar, dry-season irrigation need, rain falling on a cash crop in the flood season, bare-soil months, whether it adds a legume or breaks rice-after-rice, and for each one: why it is shown, evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks to review locally.
  • After the flood: the farmer taps the month the water went down and sees the next sowing month, harvest month, extra water needed and warnings (e.g. "soybean does not tolerate waterlogging").
  • Field greenness from space: MODIS NDVI time series (2023–2026) over rice paddies in each zone.
  • Learn: six short cards (crop rotation, why soybean helps, rice under water, El Niño, what the satellite sees, what to do when the water goes down), each with a source and a read-aloud button, plus a plain-language glossary (mm, ET0, Kc, NDVI).
  • Take the plan to your technician: one tap sends a summary by WhatsApp. Nothing the farmer selects is stored.

How it works (methods)

  • Climate: NASA POWER 2001–2025 monthly climatology (AG community) for each zone; rain = PRECTOTCORR × days in month; temperature corrected from grid-cell to field elevation with a 6.5 °C/km lapse rate.
  • ET0: Hargreaves (FAO-56) using T2M, T2M_RANGE and top-of-atmosphere radiation from NASA POWER.
  • Crop water use: ETc = Kc × ET0, with FAO-56 Table 12 crop coefficients stored in data/crops.csv. Dry-season irrigation need = Σ max(0, Kc × ET0 − rain), May–December.
  • Example (Daule, June–September): dry-season rice needs ≈ 748 mm of irrigation; soybean ≈ 553 mm, about 26% less water.
  • NDVI: MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 (250 m, 16-day), median of a 3×3 pixel window over verified paddy locations, keeping only good/marginal pixels (cloud-filtered).

Honest limits (shown in the app)

NASA POWER is zone-level (~50 km grid): Daule, Salitre and Samborondón share one grid cell, so NDVI (250 m) is what tells them apart. Hargreaves can overestimate ET0 in humid climates; the water balance ignores soil storage and paddy percolation. Cloud cover leaves gaps in NDVI and in the flood map (shown as "no data", never as zero). Missing crop data are shown as information gaps. Every option is labelled "review with a local technician".

Benefits and intended impact

The tool helps a farmer see, before investing, how much money and water each strategy puts at risk, and gives a concrete plan after a flood. Rice → soybean can cut dry-season water need and add a legume that breaks rice monoculture. It is built for low-cost phones, in Spanish, with audio, and with no account or personal data. The method works anywhere NASA data exist: new Coast zones only need new coordinates. Extending it to the Andes would require other crops (potato, maize, quinoa), other risks (frost, drought, erosion) and finer data than the 50 km climate grid.

Tools and technologies

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Leaflet maps, Chart.js charts, PapaParse) hosted free on GitHub Pages; Python in Google Colab to download and process NASA data (NASA POWER API, MODIS via Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC); CSV files in a public GitHub repository as the data layer; NASA GIBS WMTS tiles loaded live. Code: https://github.com/milkyway3257/Warpdrive-spaceapps-2026

What makes it creative

It joins a 25-year climate baseline, live flood imagery and satellite crop greenness into one decision a farmer can act on, adds an "after the flood" planner instead of only before-season advice, and is designed for people who may not read well: bilingual, read-aloud learning cards and WhatsApp sharing.

Team

  • Alejandro Avelino – team captain and integrator: user and problem definition, specification, app development (with AI assistance) and pitch.
  • Diego Lino – NASA data: NASA POWER climate for the four zones with elevation correction; MODIS NDVI time series, re-processed over verified rice paddies with cloud filtering.
  • Isaac Aguilar – agronomy: crop table (FAO-56 Kc, tolerances, sources), the three rotation strategies with evidence, gaps and risks, and plain-language glossary.
  • Bryan Álvarez – user testing and presentation support.

Use of AI (SI) – disclosure

The idea, user, region and strategies were chosen by the team. AI assistants (Claude, Gemini) were used for research support, writing and debugging code, data-processing scripts, translation and text editing; all AI-assisted code files carry an "SI disclosure" note and the app footer states it. The demo video uses an AI-generated voiceover, marked on screen. No NASA logos or branding are used.
